lastText: File ClosedWhat the Steppe KeptContestedSoviet High Command, 1939–1945End of hostilities: OCTOBER 1945 (PROJECTED) · filed with minor delayImmediate AftermathVictory in Europe arrives around October 1945: later than the historical May 1945, the price of choices that spent time to save men. The army that reaches Berlin has paid for the ground twice over: a war fought closer to the historical pattern of holding rigid lines regardless of the arithmetic, at the cost this campaign keeps returning to. The tank armies waited for the three fronts to close together and entered Prague on May 11, two days later than they did in the real war. The Seelow Heights fell on the second day instead of the third, at a lower cost: the best the plan could have done, and not what happened. The push straight for Berlin in February was actually attempted here: testing Chuikov's postwar claim against the flank risk Zhukov's own staff warned about, rather than leaving the question a memoir argument. Germany's defeat was not a variable Soviet command decisions controlled, only its timing and its price.One Year LaterVictory arrived behind the historical May 1945, which means Soviet forces are still consolidating a front the historical record had a year's head start settling by this point. Within the year, the governments this front's advance put in place across Eastern Europe are consolidating along lines this campaign's own choices shaped only at the margins: the deeper political outcome was set well be
